title: Acquired hepatocerebral degeneration: A case report
case_prompt:
A 51-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B virus infection presented with a 1-year history of progressive cognitive difficulties. He began having trouble driving, became lost on familiar streets, repeatedly forgot recent events, and later was unable to meet work commitments, leading to job loss. Over the past 3 months, he developed visual hallucinations—seeing dancers on his computer screen and “Indians” running around his house—along with confabulations, lack of initiative, and emotional blunting. Concurrently, he noted tremor of both arms and hands, gait instability, slowed movements, and intermittent “shock-like” jerks in his arms.

His medical history included chronic HBV infection since 2009, mild hepatic dysfunction (Child-Pugh score 6, class A), treatment with interferon and tenofovir, and a liver biopsy showing mild cirrhosis.

On neurologic examination, he had an unsteady gait without arm swing, bilateral symmetric rest and postural tremor of the arms, mild rigidity, and negative myoclonus on outstretched arms. He exhibited facial hypomimia and dysarthric speech. His Mini-Mental State Examination score was 19/30, down from 30/30 one year earlier. Neuropsychological testing revealed severe deficits in motor function, constructional abilities, attention, working memory, visual episodic memory, and auditory-verbal learning, as well as mild to moderate impairments in initiation/perseveration, visual search, reasoning/abstraction, verbal episodic memory, verbal fluency, and naming.

Laboratory studies showed an elevated serum ammonia level of 109 µmol/L (reference 11–32 µmol/L). Serum copper, ceruloplasmin, and urinary copper levels were normal. 

Brain MRI demonstrated mild cortical and subcortical atrophy on T1-weighted images and bilateral symmetrical hyperintensities in the globus pallidus, substantia nigra (including the ventral midbrain), and hypothalamus; the putamen, caudate, thalamus, red nucleus, and cerebellum were spared. T2-weighted images showed small foci of hyperintensity in the subcortical and deep white matter. MR spectroscopy revealed no increase in glutamate–glutamine peaks and a decrease in myo-inositol and choline resonances. 

Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler showed a cirrhotic liver without evidence of a portosystemic venous shunt.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Wilson disease was considered but excluded — “The results of serum copper and ceruloplasmin levels and urinary copper were normal.”  
2. Hepatic encephalopathy was considered but deemed unlikely — “MR spectroscopy peaks showed no increase in Glx, a typical finding in hepatic encephalopathy…”  
3. Portosystemic shunting was evaluated but not detected — “Abdominal ultrasonography with Color Doppler demonstrated a cirrhotic liver but showed no portosystemic venous shunt,” although micro-shunts may be undetectable.
